title: DNS Zone Transfer over TLS
summary: DNS zone transfers are sent in cleartext, so eavesdroppers can collect a zone's contents, and TSIG authorizes clients but does not add confidentiality. This document specifies using TLS for zone transfers, called XFR over TLS (XoT). It also updates RFC 1995, RFC 5936 and RFC 7766 on efficient use of TCP connections.

plainLanguage.summary:
A DNS zone transfer copies a zone, or its recent changes, from a primary name server to a secondary one. RFC 9103 runs those transfers inside TLS 1.3, usually on port 853, so that someone watching the network cannot collect the whole list of names and addresses.

Every server that shares a zone has to agree to use it. One server that still transfers in the clear is enough to expose the zone.

subtitle: Encrypting DNS zone transfers, both full and incremental, with TLS 1.3 so that a passive observer cannot collect a zone.

tldr.problem: DNS zone transfers normally travel in cleartext, so anyone watching the network can collect the full contents of a zone. TSIG authorizes clients but does not encrypt anything.
tldr.mechanism: XFR over TLS (XoT) runs AXFR and IXFR inside TLS 1.3, normally on port 853, with the ALPN token dot, strict server authentication and client authorization by mutual TLS or by an IP access list plus TSIG or SIG(0). The document also tightens TCP connection reuse for all zone transfers.
tldr.outcome: Zone contents are protected from passive surveillance, but only if the whole transfer group uses XoT. It does not hide that a zone exists, who hosts it, or how much the zone changes.

today: RFC 9103 was published in August 2021 and is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 1995, RFC 5936 and RFC 7766.

sections.title: Why Zone Transfers Need Encryption
sections.content:
A DNS zone is the list of names and addresses for one part of the DNS tree. A zone transfer copies that list from a primary name server to a secondary one. The original transfer mechanisms, AXFR for a full copy and IXFR for the recent changes, travel over TCP in the clear, so anyone watching the network can collect the whole zone.

The zone can reveal more than addresses. Host names often include people's names, service names that give away locations, and references to other organisations. The full contents expose every IP address in the records, which helps an attacker choose targets, especially for IPv6 addresses and private networks. There may also be regulatory or policy reasons to treat the zone as private.

RFC 5936 specifies TSIG for authorising transfer clients and for data integrity, but it asks for no confidentiality, and TSIG does not encrypt. This document specifies running both transfers inside TLS, which it calls XFR over TLS (XoT).
sections.plainLanguage: A zone transfer copies a list of DNS names and addresses from one name server to another. The copy travels in the clear, so anyone watching the network can collect the whole list. That list often contains names of people, of places and of other organisations, plus every address in use.

sections.title: The Threat Model and What It Leaves Out
sections.content:
The threat model treats the current contents and the size of a zone as sensitive, and the transfer as the point where they leak. It deliberately excludes other information. The existence of a zone, the fact that a transfer happens, and the identities of the name servers that hold it are not treated as sensitive, and XoT does not try to hide them.

The reasons given are practical. Much of that information can be found by active scanning of the DNS, and an attacker who can watch traffic can infer the relationships between name servers from the traffic patterns even when the traffic is encrypted. The model also does not cover attacks on the messages that trigger a transfer, such as NOTIFY.

There is a related problem the RFC does not solve: zone enumeration. A signed zone that uses NSEC records lets a client walk the whole zone by asking for the denial-of-existence records. NSEC3 makes that harder but has been shown to be breakable. Preventing eavesdropping on transfers and preventing enumeration are separate problems that happen to protect the same information.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC protects the zone contents as they are copied. It does not hide that a zone exists, that a transfer happened, or which servers hold it. A separate problem, walking a zone by asking for its denial-of-existence records, is also left alone.

sections.title: How Zone Transfers Work Today
sections.content:
The original specifications were built on a polling model: a secondary queries for the SOA record, the record that marks the start of the zone's authority, and decides from that whether a full transfer is needed. IXFR and NOTIFY, added by RFC 1995 and RFC 1996, let changes propagate promptly, and have largely replaced full transfers for dynamically updated zones. RFC 5936 then rewrote the AXFR specification for better performance and interoperability.

In XoT the secondary is the TLS client and the primary is the TLS server, because the secondary opens the connection. The NOTIFY and the SOA query stay outside TLS, over UDP, or travel inside the TLS session. Only the AXFR or IXFR request and its response need to be inside TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: A secondary server asks for the zone's start-of-authority record to see whether it needs a copy, and the primary sends a notification when something changes. With XoT the secondary opens the encrypted connection, so it is the TLS client and the primary is the TLS server.

sections.title: Connection Reuse for Zone Transfers
sections.content:
The document also updates how zone transfers use TCP. RFC 1995 and RFC 5936 predate TCP becoming a normal DNS transport, and many implementations still open a connection for one transfer and close it afterwards. The RFC now says implementations MUST follow RFC 7766 to optimise the use of TCP connections, and SHOULD use the edns-tcp-keepalive EDNS(0) option from RFC 7828 to manage persistent connections.

A client SHOULD reuse an existing open connection to the same primary for new transfer requests and for SOA queries, and the number of connections between a secondary and a primary SHOULD be minimised. There are valid reasons not to reuse one: separate connections for different zones, a limit on outstanding requests, an exhausted message ID pool, repeated timeouts, or a server that has signalled it wants the connection closed.

Servers MUST handle several concurrent transfers on one connection, for the same zone and for different zones, and SHOULD send responses as soon as they are ready, which may put them out of order. A client that pipelines transfer requests MUST be able to handle intermingled responses. Clients MAY choose not to pipeline transfers, because transfers are not latency sensitive and are harder to handle, and in that case they will never receive out-of-order responses.
sections.plainLanguage: Zone transfers should share one connection instead of opening a new one each time. The server must cope with several transfers at once on that connection, and it may answer them out of order.

sections.title: How XoT Works
sections.content:
The client MUST select the ALPN token dot during the TLS handshake, and implementations MUST use TLS 1.3 or later. The connection SHOULD be established on port 853, unless the primary and secondary agree on another port; they may also agree on different ports for AXoT and IXoT, or for different zones.

For a transfer to count as protected, every request and response for that zone MUST travel over TLS. At a minimum, the client MUST authenticate the server using an authentication domain name with a Strict Privacy profile as described in RFC 8310, and the server MUST check that the client is allowed to transfer the zone, using mutual TLS, or an IP-based access control list combined with a valid TSIG or SIG(0) signature on the request. If only one of those two methods is used, mutual TLS is preferred, because it protects both ends cryptographically.

If a server receives a query on a TLS connection that it is not willing to answer there, it SHOULD reply with REFUSED and the extended DNS error code 21, Not Supported, as defined in RFC 8914. Clients should then stop sending that kind of query to the server for a reasonable period, for example an hour, long enough for the configuration or policy to change.
sections.plainLanguage: The secondary opens a TLS 1.3 connection on port 853 and asks for the zone. The server must confirm the secondary's identity with a certificate, either directly or by checking its address and a signature on the request. Anything the server does not want to answer over TLS is refused with a specific error code, so the client can stop asking.

sections.title: Padding, Policy and Migration
sections.content:
Padding is offered as a way to hide how much data moved. AXoT responses can be padded so that the total size of the zone and the size of each change are harder to measure, and IXoT responses can be padded so that the activity and growth of the zone are harder to measure. The RFC deliberately leaves the exact padding policies to later work, but requires that secondaries cope with padded responses, including empty AXoT responses that carry only a padding option and no records.

Policy is an operational matter rather than a protocol one. All the servers that transfer a given set of zones form a transfer group, and the whole group MUST have a consistent policy of using XoT; if any member does not, that member is the weak point. Within a transfer group, both full and incremental transfers for a zone must use XoT. The policy must state whether mutual TLS is used, or the combination of an address list and TSIG or SIG(0). Because the servers in a group may sit under different operators, enforcing that consistency can be hard in practice.

For migration, servers may offer a per-zone option letting a specific client use either XoT or plain TCP, and clients may offer options for the multi-primary case where some primaries have moved to XoT and others have not. The RFC says such options should only be used in a migration mode and with great care. It also notes that putting a TLS proxy in front of the primary is a simple way to enable XoT on the server side.
sections.plainLanguage: Padding can make the size of a transfer less revealing, but the rules for how much padding to add are left for later. Every server that shares a zone must agree to use the encrypted transfer, because one server that does not is enough to leak the contents.

sections.title: Authentication Mechanisms
sections.content:
The RFC classifies the available mechanisms by three properties. Data origin authentication means the message really came from the party that holds the shared credentials, and that its contents were not altered. Channel confidentiality means the two ends of the connection cannot be read by a passive observer. Channel authentication means each end knows the identity of the other end of the connection.

  • TSIG signs the DNS message with a shared secret. It gives data origin authentication on both sides, but no confidentiality.
  • Strict TLS means the client is configured with an authentication domain name, and possibly a public key pin, and refuses to continue if the server cannot be authenticated. It gives channel confidentiality and channel authentication of the server.
  • Mutual TLS extends Strict TLS with a client certificate, so both ends authenticate each other.
  • An IP-based access control list on the primary restricts which addresses may request a transfer. It gives channel authentication of the client, but only once a request has arrived on the connection.

Two combinations are enough on their own: mutual TLS alone, because both ends are cryptographically authenticated, or Strict TLS on the secondary side combined with an IP-based list and TSIG or SIG(0) on the primary side. An IP-based list alone can be defeated by spoofing addresses, and TSIG alone is weak if a message is ever sent in the clear by a server that holds the key.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four ways to check who is on the other end, and they protect different things. A signature on the message proves who wrote it but hides nothing. A server certificate proves who is on the other end and hides the content. A client certificate proves who is on the other end as well. An address list on the server only proves it once the request has arrived.

sections.title: What XoT Still Leaves Open
sections.content:
XoT protects against one specific risk: an attacker collecting whole zones by eavesdropping on cleartext zone transfers. It does not mitigate three others.

  • The size and timing of transfers on an encrypted connection can still reveal that a zone is active and how much it is changing, especially when combined with SOA records fetched by querying the authoritative servers directly.
  • Hidden primaries can still be inferred or identified by watching encrypted connections.
  • Zone contents can still be obtained by zone enumeration.

The RFC points to RFC 7858 and RFC 8310 for the security concerns of DNS over TLS itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The transfer itself is hidden now. What it does not hide is that the zone changed, how much it changed, or the fact that a hidden primary exists. Walking the zone by other means still works too.
